levels.title_en: The family, and the gender problem

items.pronunciation_notes: The final inherent vowel drops, so the word is parivaar rather than parivaara.

learn.explanation_en: परिवार is the general word for a family, the group rather than the building they live in. It is masculine, and its plural looks exactly like its singular, which is true of every masculine noun that does not end in -ा. Watch out here: this word ends in a consonant, and consonant endings tell you nothing at all about gender. किताब also ends in a consonant and is feminine. With words like this the gender has to be learned alongside the meaning.

examples.note: बड़ा takes its masculine form because परिवार is masculine.
छोटा ends in -ा for the same reason.
A very common phrase, used for the family gathered together.

common_error.why_en: परिवार is masculine despite its consonant ending, so the adjective takes -ा rather than -ी.

practice.question: परिवार
practice.explanation_en: परिवार is the family as a group of people. घर is the house they live in.

game.question_en: राम ___ परिवार — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: परिवार is masculine and singular, so the form is का. Its consonant ending gives no clue, so this one is memorised.

items.pronunciation_notes: The crescent nasalises the vowel — the aa hums through the nose and no n is pronounced.

learn.explanation_en: माँ is the everyday word for mother, warm and used directly in address. It is feminine, and here is the first real trap in this module: the word ends in the आ sound, which normally signals a masculine noun. This one does not follow that pattern, so its gender has to be learned rather than worked out. The more formal माता appears in writing and in the fixed pair माता-पिता, meaning parents.

examples.note: अच्छी ends in -ी because माँ is feminine.
A fixed pair joining the formal words for mother and father.
Feminine nouns not ending in -ी take -एँ in the plural.

common_error.why_en: माँ ends in the आ sound but is feminine, so the adjective takes -ी.

practice.question: माँ
practice.explanation_en: माँ is mother. बहन is sister and बेटी is daughter.

game.question_en: राम ___ माँ — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: माँ is feminine, so की — even though its आ ending would normally point towards a masculine noun.

items.pronunciation_notes: Dental त with the tongue on the teeth, and a long final vowel: pitaa.

learn.explanation_en: पिता is the word for father used in writing and in respectful speech, while पापा is what most people actually say at home. It is masculine and ends in -ा, which is the ordinary masculine pattern, so for once the ending predicts the gender correctly. It does have one oddity worth noting now: unlike most -ा masculines it never changes to -े, so its plural looks identical to its singular.

examples.note: The same fixed pair, now from the other side.
जी is added to kinship terms to show respect.
The adjective ends in -ा, matching the masculine noun.

practice.question: पिता
practice.explanation_en: पिता is father. दादा is a grandfather and चाचा an uncle.

game.question_en: राम ___ पिता — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: पिता is masculine and singular, so का. The -ा ending points the right way here, unlike in माँ.

summary.recap_en: This level began the family words with परिवार, माँ and पिता, and introduced the rule that runs through the whole module: every Hindi noun carries a gender, and only some endings tell you what it is.
summary.next_up_en: Next: भाई and बहन, including one word whose ending actively points the wrong way.

items.pronunciation_notes: Breathy भ, then a long aa and a long ii — bhaaii, said as two clear beats.

learn.explanation_en: भाई means brother, and it doubles as a way of addressing any man of roughly your own age, rather as English uses 'mate'. It is masculine, and this is the ending that misleads English speakers most often: -ी normally marks feminine nouns, so भाई looks feminine and is not. आदमी, meaning man, and पानी, meaning water, are masculine for exactly the same reason. All three have to be learned as exceptions.

examples.note: Hindi marks older and younger siblings separately.
The adjective takes -ा because भाई is masculine.
The plural is identical to the singular.

common_error.why_en: भाई ends in -ी but is masculine, so the adjective takes -ा.

practice.question: भाई
practice.explanation_en: भाई is brother. बहन is sister and बेटा is son.

game.question_en: राम ___ भाई — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: भाई is masculine, so का — even though the -ी ending looks feminine. This is the single commonest gender mistake English speakers make.

items.pronunciation_notes: Two syllables, bahan. In the plural the middle vowel disappears: बहनें is bahneṁ, not bahaneṁ.

learn.explanation_en: बहन is sister, and like भाई it doubles as a respectful way to address a woman you do not know. It is feminine and ends in a consonant, which as usual tells you nothing about its gender. Notice what happens in the plural: बहनें is said 'bahneṁ' with the middle vowel gone, which is exactly the medial schwa behaviour from the last module showing up in ordinary vocabulary.

examples.note: बड़ी takes -ी because बहन is feminine.
The counterpart to छोटा भाई from the last card.
Feminine nouns ending in a consonant take -एँ in the plural.

practice.question: बहन
practice.explanation_en: बहन is sister. बेटी is daughter and पत्नी is wife.

game.question_en: राम ___ बहन — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: बहन is feminine, so की. Its consonant ending predicts nothing, so this one is learned with the word.

items.pronunciation_notes: Retroflex ट with the tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth. Two syllables, beṭaa.

learn.explanation_en: बेटा means son, and it is also used affectionately to address any young person, including a girl. It is masculine and ends in -ा, so its gender is predictable for once. It is also the first noun in this module whose plural actually changes shape: masculine nouns ending in -ा take -े in the plural, which gives बेटे.

examples.note: Both words end in -ा.
The -ा becomes -े in the plural.
The two words differ only in their final vowel.

practice.question: बेटा
practice.explanation_en: बेटा is son. बच्चा is a child of either sex, and भाई is brother.

game.question_en: राम ___ बेटा — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: बेटा is masculine, so का. Here the -ा ending predicts the gender correctly.

summary.recap_en: This level added भाई, बहन and बेटा. भाई is the important one: its -ी ending looks feminine and the word is masculine, which is the mistake English speakers make most often.
summary.next_up_en: Next: बेटी, पति and पत्नी, where two endings predict correctly and one does not.

items.pronunciation_notes: The plural inserts a y sound and nasalises the ending: beṭiyãa.

learn.explanation_en: बेटी is daughter, the exact counterpart of बेटा. It ends in -ी and is feminine, so the ending predicts correctly — which is worth noticing precisely because भाई broke that pattern two cards ago. Feminine nouns ending in -ी form their plural with -ियाँ, and the long ी shortens as it does so.

examples.note: Both words end in -ी.
The -ी becomes -ियाँ in the plural.
The feminine adjective ending matches the noun.

common_error.why_en: The long ी shortens to ि before the plural ending, so बेटीयाँ is not a possible spelling.

practice.question: बेटी
practice.explanation_en: बेटी is daughter. बहन is sister and पत्नी is wife.

game.question_en: राम ___ बेटी — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: बेटी is feminine, so की. The -ी ending predicts correctly here, unlike in भाई.

items.pronunciation_notes: A short i at the end, not a long one, and a dental त with the tongue on the teeth: pati.

learn.explanation_en: पति is husband. It ends in a short -ि, an ending rare enough that it predicts nothing at all, and it happens to be masculine. Its plural does not change. Keep it clearly apart from पत्नी, meaning wife: the two look similar but they are separate words, not a masculine and feminine pair of the kind बेटा and बेटी form.

examples.note: The adjective ends in -ा, matching the masculine noun.
A very common fixed pair.
The plural is identical to the singular.

common_error.why_en: पति is masculine, so the adjective takes -ा despite the word's unusual i ending.

practice.question: पति
practice.explanation_en: पति is husband. पत्नी is wife — the two words look alike but are not masculine and feminine forms of one word.

game.question_en: राम ___ पति — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: पति is masculine, so का. Its short -ि ending gives no clue whatsoever.

items.pronunciation_notes: The त्न stack runs त straight into न with no vowel between them, giving patnii in two syllables rather than three.

learn.explanation_en: पत्नी is wife, and it carries a conjunct from the last module: त् runs straight into न, so the word is said 'patnii' rather than 'patanii'. It ends in -ी and is feminine, so the ending predicts correctly. In casual speech many people say बीवी instead, particularly in northern India, though पत्नी is what you will read.

examples.note: The same fixed pair, from the other side.
The adjective takes -ी to match.
The -ी becomes -ियाँ, exactly as in बेटियाँ.

practice.question: पत्नी
practice.explanation_en: पत्नी is wife. बहन is sister and बेटी is daughter.

game.question_en: राम ___ पत्नी — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: पत्नी is feminine, so की. The -ी ending points the right way here.

summary.recap_en: This level covered बेटी, पति and पत्नी. Two of the three have endings that predict their gender correctly, while पति ends in a short -ि that predicts nothing at all.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the grandparents, where Hindi keeps apart two relationships English runs together.

items.pronunciation_notes: Both द are dental — the tongue presses against the back of the upper teeth rather than curling back.

learn.explanation_en: Hindi splits what English calls a grandfather into two separate words: दादा is your father's father, while नाना is your mother's father. English speakers reach for the wrong one constantly, because English gives them no reason to keep the two apart, and a Hindi speaker notices the slip at once. The word is masculine and ends in -ा. Kinship terms like this usually stay unchanged in the plural out of respect, rather than taking the -े you saw in बेटे.

examples.note: जी is added to almost every kinship term in address.
Both of these are on the father's side.
बूढ़ा contains the breathy flap from Module 2.

practice.question: दादा
practice.explanation_en: दादा is specifically the father's father. The mother's father is नाना, and Hindi keeps the two sides apart.

game.question_en: राम ___ दादा — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: दादा is masculine, so का. The -ा ending predicts correctly.

items.pronunciation_notes: A long ii at the end — daadii differs from daadaa in that final vowel alone.

learn.explanation_en: दादी is your father's mother, and नानी is your mother's mother. The same split as दादा and नाना, and the same warning applies: the two are not interchangeable. A useful memory hook is that the द words belong to the father's side and the न words to the mother's. दादी is feminine and ends in -ी, so the ending predicts correctly.

examples.note: The respectful particle again.
बूढ़ी takes the feminine -ी ending.
One from each side of the family.

practice.question: दादी
practice.explanation_en: दादी is the father's mother. The mother's mother is नानी.

game.question_en: राम ___ दादी — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: दादी is feminine, so की. The -ी ending predicts correctly.

items.pronunciation_notes: The च्च stack holds the ch, with no breath on either half: bachchaa.

learn.explanation_en: बच्चा means a child, and it is grammatically masculine whatever the child's sex. That reflects a general fact about Hindi: the masculine is the default when sex is unspecified or mixed. There is a feminine form बच्ची used specifically of a girl. The plural बच्चे is one of the most common words you will hear, since it covers children in general.

examples.note: The held च्च stack from the last module.
The -ा becomes -े, exactly as in बेटे.
The adjective takes -े to match the plural noun.

practice.question: बच्चा
practice.explanation_en: बच्चा is a child of either sex. बेटा is specifically a son.

game.question_en: राम ___ बच्चा — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: बच्चा is masculine, so का — and it stays masculine even when the child being spoken about is a girl.

summary.recap_en: This level completed the family words with दादा, दादी and बच्चा. Hindi keeps the father's and mother's sides of the family apart, and बच्चा is masculine by default regardless of the child's sex.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the body, beginning with three words that all end in consonants and do not all share a gender.

items.pronunciation_notes: One syllable — the final inherent vowel drops, so the word is sir rather than sira.

learn.explanation_en: सिर is the head. It ends in a consonant, so its gender is not predictable and simply has to be learned: it is masculine. Notice the pronunciation too — the written word has two consonants but is said as a single syllable, because the final inherent vowel drops. Its plural does not change.

examples.note: The masculine adjective ending.
Two nouns side by side, both dropping their final vowels.
The plural is unchanged.

practice.question: सिर
practice.explanation_en: सिर is the head. हाथ is a hand and आँख an eye.

game.question_en: राम ___ सिर — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: सिर is masculine, so का. Its consonant ending gives no clue.

items.pronunciation_notes: The crescent nasalises the opening vowel — it hums through the nose and no n is heard. One syllable, ãakh.

learn.explanation_en: आँख is an eye. It carries the crescent from the last module, so the opening vowel is nasalised and no n sound appears anywhere in it. The word ends in a consonant and is feminine, which the ending does not tell you. You will meet the plural आँखें far more often than the singular, since eyes usually come in pairs.

examples.note: The feminine adjective, and the -एँ plural.
Feminine nouns ending in a consonant take -एँ.
काली ends in -ी because the noun is feminine.

common_error.why_en: आँख is feminine, so the adjective takes -ी in both the singular and the plural.

practice.question: आँख
practice.explanation_en: आँख is an eye. कान is an ear and सिर the head.

game.question_en: राम ___ आँख — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: आँख is feminine, so की. The consonant ending predicts nothing, so this one is learned with the word.

items.pronunciation_notes: The final थ is aspirated — the tongue is on the teeth and breath is released. One syllable, haath.

learn.explanation_en: हाथ is a hand, and in ordinary speech it often covers the arm as well. It ends in a consonant, so its gender has to be learned: masculine. Set it beside आँख from the last card — both end in consonants, and they take opposite genders. That pairing is the clearest possible demonstration of why consonant endings are marked as unpredictable all through this module.

examples.note: दायाँ carries a crescent of its own.
The plural is unchanged.
साफ़ has the dotted letter from Module 2 and never changes form.

practice.question: हाथ
practice.explanation_en: हाथ is a hand. पैर is a foot and उँगली a finger.

game.question_en: राम ___ हाथ — का, के or की?
game.explanation_en: हाथ is masculine, so का — while आँख, which also ends in a consonant, takes की.

summary.recap_en: This level began the body words with सिर, आँख and हाथ. All three end in consonants, and they do not share a gender — आँख is feminine while the other two are masculine, which is why every consonant-ending noun in this module is flagged.
summary.next_up_en: Next: more of the body, including two nouns whose endings finally give something away.
